extracted.intended_audience: general public and research community (researchers, academic administrators, funders, publishers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for evaluating research and researchers, centering on limiting use of journal impact factor and promoting more appropriate, robust assessment practices across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use journal impact factor to assess individual researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration denounces the practice of correlating the journal impact factor to the merits of a specific scientist's contributions. It states that the impact factor is not to be used as a substitute "measure of the quality of individual research articles, or in hiring, promotion, or funding decisions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: using journal impact factor creates biases and inaccuracies when appraising scientific research. Intended application: avoid using journal-level impact factors to make judgments about individual papers or people in hiring, promotion, tenure, or funding contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align measures of journal/article impact with actual journal quality and community value
rubrics_metrics.description: The group concluded that impact factors for many journals do not accurately reflect the value to the community of the work published; therefore measures of journal and article impact should be better aligned with journal quality and the value to the scholarly community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: assessment systems should examine whether chosen metrics reflect meaningful quality or contribution for the relevant field/community, and replace or supplement misleading metrics where they do not. This concern originated in cell biology but is stated to extend across all scholarly disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt practical, robust, and discipline-sensitive approaches to research assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: DORA (the organization) seeks to advance practical and robust approaches to research assessment globally and across all scholarly disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of implementation support include Project TARA (Tools to Advance Research Assessment) and the Reformscape database which collates institutional policies. Assessments should be practical (implementable) and robust (resistant to gaming or distortion) and take disciplinary differences into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should implement DORA principles in recognition, reward, hiring, and promotion policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration's principles have been adopted by institutions and funders to inform new systems of research recognition and reward that move away from reliance on impact factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dutch universities and funders introduced new recognition and reward systems based on DORA; CNRS announced individual assessment in line with DORA principles. Cautionary note: signatory status does not guarantee adherence—cases (e.g., Liverpool) show institutions may still use problematic metrics despite being signatories, prompting DORA to raise concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: DORA applies across all scholarly disciplines and to a range of actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The initiative is presented as a worldwide effort covering all scholarly disciplines and has been signed by universities, research institutes, learned societies, funding bodies, publishers, and individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for policy makers and administrators: reforms guided by DORA should consider cross-disciplinary applicability and involve diverse stakeholders (funders, publishers, societies, institutions) when redesigning assessment practices.
